title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clinical disease. Signs and symptoms have appeared.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Before disease. The person is exposed to risk factors but not yet ill.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Consequences. Chronic disability, complications, recurrence.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary prevention. Reduces incidence (new cases): immunisation, health education, smoking cessation; the most cost-effective.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secondary prevention. Early detection and intervention before clinical signs: cancer screening, TB skin tests, contact tracing.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tertiary prevention. Reduces chronic disability and recurrence: physiotherapy, rehabilitation, reintegration, palliative care, follow-up.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Subclinical phase. Disease present but without clinical signs: the window for screening.

title: Define disease prevention.
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Define disease prevention.
body.back: Measures aiming to prevent the onset of disease, stop its progress and reduce its consequences (WHO, 1984).

title: Three levels of prevention with examples?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Three levels of prevention with examples?
body.back: Primary: reduce incidence (vaccination, education, smoking cessation). Secondary: early detection (screening, TB skin tests, contact tracing). Tertiary: reduce disability/recurrence (rehab, reintegration, palliation, surveillance).

title: Conditions justifying screening?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Conditions justifying screening?
body.back: Frequent disease with excess (premature) mortality and cost; effective treatment with real benefit; feasible early mass diagnosis.

title: Define health promotion.
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Define health promotion.
body.back: The process of enabling people to increase control over their health and its determinants (Ottawa Charter, WHO 1986).

title: Prerequisites for health?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Prerequisites for health?
body.back: Peace, shelter, education, food, income, stable ecosystem, sustainable resources, social justice and equity.

title: Five pillars of health promotion?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Five pillars of health promotion?
body.back: Build healthy public policy; create supportive environments; strengthen community action; develop personal skills; reorient health services.

title: Tools for healthy public policy?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Tools for healthy public policy?
body.back: Advocacy, health impact assessment, intersectoral action.

title: Prevention vs promotion?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Prevention vs promotion?
body.back: Prevention: biomedical, vertical programmes, population as object, risk factors, individual responsibility. Promotion: bio-psycho-social, horizontal, population as subject, strengths, determinants.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Chi-square test. Association between two qualitative variables; Fisher's exact test for small samples.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Two numeric variables. E.g. age and blood pressure.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Start here. Identify variable types, study design and distribution (Shapiro-Wilk).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: One categorical, one numeric. E.g. comparing mean blood pressure between two groups.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Two categorical variables. E.g. smoking (yes/no) and disease (yes/no).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Correlation. Pearson if normal; Spearman if not.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Comparing means. Student's t-test if normal; Mann-Whitney if not.

title: Purpose of biostatistics?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Purpose of biostatistics?
body.back: To describe, compare and interpret health phenomena using data.

title: Types of variables with examples?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Types of variables with examples?
body.back: Qualitative nominal (sex, blood group), qualitative ordinal (pain scale), quantitative discrete (number of children), quantitative continuous (height, BP).

title: Three basic study designs?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Three basic study designs?
body.back: Cross-sectional (one time point), cohort (exposure → outcome over time), case-control (cases vs controls).

title: Measures of central tendency?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Measures of central tendency?
body.back: Mean (average), median (middle value), mode (most frequent); equal in a normal distribution.

title: How do you read a Shapiro-Wilk test?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: How do you read a Shapiro-Wilk test?
body.back: H₀ = normal; α = 0.05; p > 0.05 → normal; p ≤ 0.05 → not normal; W near 1 = more normal.

title: Best graph by variable type?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Best graph by variable type?
body.back: Nominal: bar/pie. Ordinal: ordered bar. Discrete: bar. Continuous: histogram, box plot.

title: Test choice decision tree?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Test choice decision tree?
body.back: 2 qualitative: chi-square/Fisher. Qual + quant: t-test (normal) / Mann-Whitney. 2 quantitative: Pearson (normal) / Spearman.

title: Why clean data?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Why clean data?
body.back: For valid, reproducible, unbiased results: check missing values, duplicates, inconsistencies, coding errors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Behaviours. What they do: smoking, physical inactivity, diet, alcohol, stress: modifiable.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Non-modifiable. Who they are: age, sex, family history, ethnic origin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Structural determinants. Environment (air, water, climate), economic, cultural and political context.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Health outcome. Determinants interact across individual, social and environmental levels.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Living and working conditions. Education, childhood experiences, housing, transport, healthy food, safety.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Social and community support. Relationships with family, friends, co-workers and community strongly affect health.

title: Define determinants of health.
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Define determinants of health.
body.back: Factors influencing the health of individuals and communities: who they are, what they do, in which conditions they live.

title: Non-modifiable CVD risk factors?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Non-modifiable CVD risk factors?
body.back: Age (> 83% of heart deaths at 65+), sex (men), family history (father < 55, mother < 65), ethnic origin.

title: Modifiable CVD risk factors?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Modifiable CVD risk factors?
body.back: Smoking, physical inactivity, poor nutrition, overweight, high BP, high LDL, uncontrolled diabetes, excess alcohol, stress.

title: Risk vs protective factors?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Risk vs protective factors?
body.back: Risk: contribute to developing or worsening conditions (family conflict, isolation). Protective: skills, strengths, resources that shield and help cope.

title: Main social determinants?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Main social determinants?
body.back: Education and childhood experiences, neighbourhood and built environment, social and community support (plus economy and policy).

title: Criticism of lifestyle-focused models?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Criticism of lifestyle-focused models?
body.back: They make individuals responsible for behaviours (tobacco, diet, obesity) that are shaped by social conditions: is that fair?

title: Levels at which determinants act?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Levels at which determinants act?
body.back: Individual, social/community, environmental and structural (policy) levels, interacting with each other.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Analytical epidemiology. The 'how': cohort and case-control studies identify risk factors and test hypotheses (e.g. air pollution cohort).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Descriptive epidemiology. Describes the who, what, where and when; identifies patterns; generates hypotheses (e.g. measles cases by age, vaccination status, place).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Experimental studies. The investigator assigns the intervention.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Observational studies. The investigator observes without assigning exposures.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Evidence pyramid. Systematic reviews, then RCTs, cohorts, case-control, case series, case reports, opinions and in vitro research.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Randomised controlled trials. Random assignment to treatment or placebo; robust evidence for new drugs and interventions.

title: Etymology and definition of epidemiology?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Etymology and definition of epidemiology?
body.back: Epi (upon) + demos (people) + logy (science). Last (1988): study of the distribution and determinants of health-related states in specified populations, applied to prevention and control.

title: Key elements of Last's definition?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Key elements of Last's definition?
body.back: Distribution (time, place, person), determinants (biological to behavioural factors), health-related states, specified populations, application to prevention and control.

title: Endemic, epidemic, pandemic?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Endemic, epidemic, pandemic?
body.back: Endemic: constant presence. Epidemic: occurrence above the expected level. Pandemic: widespread epidemic across countries or the world.

title: Historical landmarks?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Historical landmarks?
body.back: Hippocrates (environment), Ibn al-Khatib (contagion), Graunt 1662 (mortality statistics), Lind 1747 (scurvy trial), Farr (vital statistics), Snow (cholera), Doll and Hill (smoking).

title: Epidemiologist's approach?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Epidemiologist's approach?
body.back: Ask questions (what, how much, who, where, when, why) and make comparisons (diseased vs not, exposed vs not).

title: Descriptive vs analytical epidemiology?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Descriptive vs analytical epidemiology?
body.back: Descriptive: who, what, where, when → hypotheses. Analytical: how, via cohort and case-control → test hypotheses, find risk factors.

title: Classification of study designs?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Classification of study designs?
body.back: Observational (descriptive; analytical: case-control, cohort) and experimental (RCT, field trials, community trials).

title: Evidence pyramid, top to bottom?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Evidence pyramid, top to bottom?
body.back: Systematic reviews, RCTs, cohort, case-control, case series, case reports, opinions/editorials, in vitro research.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Recovery. Cured patients leave the prevalence pool.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Death. Deaths also lower prevalence.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Relationship. Longer disease duration leads to higher prevalence for the same incidence.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Incidence. Rate of new cases arising in a population at risk over a given period.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Prevalence. Frequency of existing (old and new) cases in a population at a point or over a period.

title: Define a health indicator and its uses.
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Define a health indicator and its uses.
body.back: A quantitative measure of a health condition, trend or factor; used to describe health, show changes, evaluate programmes, plan and compare.

title: Four indicator domains with examples?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Four indicator domains with examples?
body.back: Health status (life expectancy), risk factors (stunting), service coverage (antenatal care), health systems (bed density, spending % GDP).

title: Proportion, rate, ratio?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Proportion, rate, ratio?
body.back: Proportion: unitless fraction (prevalence). Rate: occurrence over time (incidence). Ratio: one quantity over another (a:b).

title: Incidence vs prevalence?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Incidence vs prevalence?
body.back: Incidence: new cases in a period among those at risk. Prevalence: existing cases at a point or over a period.

title: Point vs period prevalence?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Point vs period prevalence?
body.back: Point: at one moment ('today'). Period: over a time (annual, lifetime: 'ever had').

title: Cumulative incidence vs incidence rate?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Cumulative incidence vs incidence rate?
body.back: Cumulative incidence (risk): new cases / population at risk at start, closed cohort. Incidence rate (density): new cases / disease-free person-time.

title: Relation between incidence and prevalence?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Relation between incidence and prevalence?
body.back: In a stable population, prevalence ≈ incidence × duration; longer duration → higher prevalence.

title: Crude, cause-specific mortality and case fatality?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Crude, cause-specific mortality and case fatality?
body.back: Crude: all deaths / population. Cause-specific: deaths from one cause / population. Case fatality: deaths among cases (severity), usually %.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Clinical medicine. Targets sick people when they consult; care at the moment of contact; the doctor holds the power; costs rarely considered.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Definition of health. WHO Constitution (1948): complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Organised efforts. Collaboration across institutions, communities and policies (e.g. COVID-19: ICU capacity, masks, vaccination).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Public health. Targets the whole population, even non-consulters, throughout life; considers costs; needs population participation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Prevention. Acts before disease develops by reducing risk factors and detecting early signs (e.g. blood pressure screening).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Health promotion. Empowers people to adopt healthier behaviours and builds supportive environments (parks, school meals, campaigns).

title: WHO definition of health?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: WHO definition of health?
body.back: A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity (WHO Constitution, 1948).

title: Winslow's definition of public health?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Winslow's definition of public health?
body.back: The science and art of preventing disease, prolonging life and promoting health through the organised efforts and informed choices of society, organisations, communities and individuals.

title: Clinical vs public health approach?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Clinical vs public health approach?
body.back: Clinical: sick people, when they consult, at contact, costs ignored, doctor's power. Public health: whole population, lifelong, costs considered, population participation.

title: Three pillars in the CVD example?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Three pillars in the CVD example?
body.back: Prevention (screening, risk factors), health promotion (supportive environments), organised efforts (policies, sectors, community).

title: Holistic management of the ER case?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Holistic management of the ER case?
body.back: Treat the wound, psychological support, social intervention, multidisciplinary coordination and continuity of care.

title: Eras of public health history?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Eras of public health history?
body.back: Sanitation (Greeks, Romans, Arab medicine, 1848 Act), environmental (1840-70: Chadwick, Snow, Virchow), bacteriological (1880-1930: Pasteur, Koch), therapeutic (1930-: insulin, sulphonamides).

title: Current public health issues?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Current public health issues?
body.back: NCDs (70% of deaths), infections (COVID-19, emerging diseases, AMR), inequalities, climate change, mental health crisis.

title: Criteria of a public health problem?
subject: subj:pubhealth1

body.front: Criteria of a public health problem?
body.back: Inequalities and vulnerabilities (e.g. TB in the poor) and social perception requiring a collective response (e.g. HIV/AIDS).
